newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sanlam calls for details on SAfrican economic plan.
newsitem.headline: Sanlam calls for details on SAfrican economic plan.

text.p: Lack of detail about how the government's five-year macro-economic strategy would be implemented had created scepticism about whether it would succeed, Sanlam chief economist Johan Louw said.
"Although we are generally in agreement with the policy framework, it is imperative that government proceeds with the implementation," Louw said in his latest economic survey.
"Such actions must be clear and credible in order to enhance confidence. There should be no doubt about the government's full commitment to the objectives," he said.
South Africa was now clearly part of the global economy and could not afford uncertainty in the international community about its financial and economic policy.
Louw said fiscal discipline would be vital to ensure the reduction of the budget deficit from 5.1 percent in 1996/97 to three percent in 1999/2000.
"We are, however, sceptical of the feasibility of a three percent deficit, and of the chances of making the labour market more flexible," he said.
The privatisation of state assets could make a significant contribution, but detailed plans to achieve privatisation and the key objectives of the new macro-economic framework were still lacking.

"Whether we will succeed in creating a more flexible labour market, promoting labour productivity and bringing about more moderate wage and price increases will depend largely on whether the proposed national so-called accord between business, labour and government will meet with success," Louw said.
Another important element would be creating a favourable investment climate "in view of the large amounts of foreign capital that will be required to supplement our poor domestic savings."
This called for a reduction in crime and unrest to a more acceptable level and co-operation between business and labour to increase the competitiveness of the economy.
